scenes.heading: Divisibility rules and digit puzzles
scenes.say: Can you tell if a big number divides by eight, eleven or twelve without dividing? Divisibility tests let you check just part of the number. In this video you will learn the tests, why they work, and how to crack missing-digit puzzles.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A bouncer checks your ID, not your whole life story
scenes.science: A test checks part of a number: last digits or digit sum
scenes.breaks: A bouncer can be fooled by a fake ID. A correct divisibility test is never wrong.
scenes.say: A bouncer at the door just checks your ID card, not your whole life story. A divisibility test is the same: a quick check on part of the number, like the last digits or the digit sum. Some doors need two checks. For twelve, you must pass the test for three and the test for four.

scenes.heading: The tests
points: 4: last two digits; 8: last three digits
7: double last digit, subtract from rest
scenes.say: For four, check the last two digits. For eight, check the last three. For three and nine, add the digits. For eleven, alternate: take away, add, take away, from the ones digit. For twelve, pass three and four. And for seven, double the last digit and subtract it from the rest.

scenes.heading: Why the digit sum works
scenes.say: Why does the digit sum work? A three-digit number is one hundred a plus ten b plus c. That equals ninety-nine a plus nine b, which is always a multiple of nine, plus the digit sum. So only the digit sum decides.
scenes.caption: 100a + 10b + c = 99a + 9b + (a + b + c)

scenes.heading: Missing-digit puzzle
scenes.question: 52_6 is divisible by 12. Find the missing digit.
scenes.say: Fifty-two blank six is divisible by twelve. Twelve is three times four, so pass both tests. For four, the last two digits must be a multiple of four, so the digit is odd. For three, thirteen plus the digit must be a multiple of three: two, five or eight. Only five is in both lists.

scenes.heading: Combining tests
scenes.say: Only combine tests with co-prime factors, ones that share nothing but one. Three and four work for twelve. Two and six do not: eighteen divides by two and six, but not twelve.

Remember: two digits for four, three digits for eight. Sum for three and nine, swing for eleven. Combine only co-prime tests. And in puzzles, test every digit from zero to nine. Now try the practice questions!
